fields.meta_title: Contest Entry Form Builder With Entry Rules | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build a contest entry form that checks eligibility and tags repeat entries, with every entry saved in a database you own.
fields.h1: Build a Contest Entry Form That Counts Only Valid Entries
fields.hero_description: Describe the contest and its rules. Emergent builds the contest entry form and the entries table behind it, with a draw or judging view for when entries close.
fields.features_heading: What a Template Leaves You to Check by Hand
fields.features_subheading: A template collects names and emails. These six pieces run the checks organizers usually do in a spreadsheet afterward.
fields.feature_1:
Eligibility checked before submit

Ask for a birth date and a state, and the form turns away anyone under your minimum age or outside the area your rules allow. An ineligible entry never reaches the draw.
fields.feature_2:
Repeat entries tagged as duplicates

Match each new entry on email or phone against everyone who has already entered. A second entry from one address is saved with a duplicate tag and left out of the count.
fields.feature_3:
Entries held to your rules on upload

Accept the entry itself as a file or as pasted text. Set a word limit or a file type, and an entry that breaks it goes back to the entrant with the reason before it is saved.
fields.feature_4:
A random draw with alternates

Draw a winner and as many alternates as your rules name, picked at random from valid entries only. Each draw is logged with its time and the entry count it drew from.
fields.feature_5:
Rules acceptance stored with each entry

Link the official rules beside a required checkbox. Every entry row keeps the version of the rules the entrant accepted and the time of submission, for any dispute later.
fields.feature_6:
The codebase is yours to keep

Export the full code to your GitHub on paid plans when a giveaway grows into a yearly program. Your developers can host it on their own servers and reuse it next season.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Contests That Run on Entry Rules
fields.tab_content_1:
Draw from 1,284 entries after repeats drop out

Northwind Coffee Roasters runs a holiday giveaway for a year of coffee, open to US residents aged 18 and over. The form allows one entry per email. Of 1,316 entries, 32 repeat an address already entered and carry a duplicate tag. The draw picks one winner and two alternates from the 1,284 that remain.
fields.tab_content_2:
Every word over 2,500 sends the story back

Stories for the Lakeside Library teen contest have a 2,500-word limit. Writers paste the story into the form, which counts the words before it accepts the entry. Entry 0147 came in at 2,740 and went back with a note to cut 240. The writer's birth date sets the age bracket the judges read it in.
fields.tab_content_3:
A bonus entry for each friend, up to five

Every listener who enters the Signal Hour gear giveaway gets a personal share link. Each friend who enters through that link adds one bonus entry, capped at five. Priya Nair brought in 7 friends and holds 6 entries in the draw: her own and 5 bonus.
fields.tab_content_4:
One vote per resident, and 412 votes pick the mural

Three mural designs made the final round of the Millbrook town contest. Residents vote once, and a vote counts only after they click the link sent to their email. Voting closed with 1,006 votes. The Harbor design won with 412 votes to Orchard's 389, and Foundry finished on 205.

fields.howto_title: How to Build a Contest Entry Form
fields.howto_description: Settle the rules before the builder opens. The form enforces what they say.
fields.howto_step_1_des: Set out who can enter, the entry period, the prize, and how the winner is picked before any field exists. A contest judged on skill states its judging criteria. A sweepstakes says how the random draw works. Every check in the form comes from this page.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Pick a minimum age and the states or countries your rules allow. Add a birth date field and a location field so the form can test both before an entry is saved. Exclude staff and their households if the rules say so.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Choose one entry per person, or one plus a bonus entry for each referral. Decide which field identifies a person: email is the usual choice, and a phone number is harder to repeat. Write the limit into the rules in the same words.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Paste the rules into one prompt and say what an entry contains, such as a story or a design file. Emergent builds the form and the entries table, with a review view for your team. Ask for a change and the form updates.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Choose a draw or a judging panel
fields.howto_step_5_des: A sweepstakes needs a random draw from valid entries, with alternates in case a winner does not reply. A skill contest needs a judging view where each judge scores every entry against the criteria written in your rules.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Plan the close and the winner email
fields.howto_step_6_des: Pick the exact closing minute and name its time zone in the rules. Write the email the winner receives, with a deadline to reply. Alternates get their own message, sent only when a winner lets that deadline pass without an answer.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Enter twice from one email before launch and confirm the second entry carries a duplicate tag. Then enter as someone under the age limit. Run a test draw on a copy of the table and read the winner email as a winner would.

plan.angle: The live top 10 is template galleries and how-to posts from WordPress form plugins and form builders (Formidable, WPForms, Gravity Forms, Jotform, Youform), plus Pinterest boards and stock vector art. The AI Overview lists the fields: name, email, phone, age, an upload and a rules checkbox. Every result stops at collecting entries. This page shows the part organizers do by hand afterward: turning away entrants who do not qualify, catching repeat entries, holding a written entry to its word limit, counting referral bonus entries up to a cap and running a public vote with one vote per person, with every entry kept as a row the organizer owns. The FAQ answers the setup, giveaway and template questions searchers ask.
tab_stories: A coffee roaster's holiday giveaway takes one entry per email address, marks 32 repeat entries as duplicates, and draws one winner and two alternates from the 1,284 entries that remain.

A public library's teen short story contest caps stories at 2,500 words, sends back a 2,740-word story with a note to cut 240 words, and sorts entrants into a 13 to 15 or 16 to 18 bracket from their birth date.
A podcast's gear giveaway gives each entrant a share link and one bonus entry per friend who enters through it, so an entrant who brings in 7 friends stops at the cap of 5 bonus entries.
A town's mural design contest lets residents vote once per confirmed email for one of three finalists, and the design with 412 of the 1,006 votes wins when voting closes.
